title: Jeremiah 51:33–44
context: The LORD of Armies pictures Babylon as a threshing floor ready for harvest (51:33). Zion’s inhabitants lament that Nebuchadnezzar devoured them (51:34–35), and the LORD answers that he will plead their cause (51:36–40). A lament over Sheshach, set in parallel with Babylon (51:41; compare 25:26), leads to the judgment of Bel (51:44). Many interpreters explain Sheshach as a coded form of Babylon’s name; that explanation is held with caution.

verses.text: For the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel says: “The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time when it is trodden. Yet a little while, and the time of harvest comes for her.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor at the time when it is trodden.” Arminian readers see Babylon ripe for judgment, its harvest time soon to come.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the threshing image of judgment. “Yet a little while” stresses that the time is near, and readers in this tradition see the LORD appointing the hour.

verses.text: “Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon has devoured me. He has crushed me. He has made me an empty vessel. He has, like a monster, swallowed me up. He has filled his mouth with my delicacies. He has cast me out.
verses.arminianNotes: “Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon has devoured me.” The WEB marks this as the voice of Zion. Arminian readers see the people voicing the trauma of conquest and exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the lament of Zion over Nebuchadnezzar’s devouring. Readers in this tradition note the vivid image of a monster swallowing its prey, giving voice to the people’s suffering.

verses.text: May the violence done to me and to my flesh be on Babylon!” the inhabitant of Zion will say; and, “May my blood be on the inhabitants of Chaldea!” will Jerusalem say.
verses.arminianNotes: “May the violence done to me and to my flesh be on Babylon!” the inhabitant of Zion will say. Arminian readers hear an appeal for justice handed over to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear Jerusalem’s plea for justice. Readers in this tradition commonly see such prayers as entrusting vengeance to God rather than taking it personally.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says: “Behold, I will plead your cause, and take vengeance for you. I will dry up her sea, and make her fountain dry.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, I will plead your cause, and take vengeance for you.” Arminian readers see the LORD answering Zion’s plea and taking up his people’s cause.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God responding to his people’s cry. Readers in both traditions commonly see shared ground here: the LORD is the defender of the oppressed.

verses.text: Babylon will become heaps, a dwelling place for jackals, an astonishment, and a hissing, without inhabitant.
verses.arminianNotes: “Babylon will become heaps, a dwelling place for jackals.” Arminian readers see the stock imagery of desolation used to describe Babylon’s ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the language of total ruin. Readers in this tradition note that the same images were used of Jerusalem in 9:11, now applied to Babylon in a reversal.

verses.text: They will roar together like young lions. They will growl as lions’ cubs.
verses.arminianNotes: “They will roar together like young lions. They will growl as lions’ cubs.” Arminian readers see Babylon’s leaders pictured as hungry lions, eager for prey.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the lion image describing Babylon’s rapacity. Readers in this tradition see it leading into the next verse, where the LORD prepares a feast that ends in their downfall.

verses.text: When they are inflamed, I will make their feast, and I will make them drunk, that they may rejoice, and sleep a perpetual sleep, and not wake up,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: “When they are inflamed, I will make their feast, and I will make them drunk … and sleep a perpetual sleep.” Arminian readers see judgment coming in the midst of revelry.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD turning Babylon’s feast into its downfall. Some readers compare Belshazzar’s feast in Daniel 5, cited by reference, though readers in this tradition hold the connection as suggestive.

verses.text: “I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams with male goats.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter, like rams with male goats.” Arminian readers see the powerful brought low, pictured as animals led to slaughter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reversal of the lions of 51:38, now led like lambs. Readers in this tradition read the image soberly as prophetic judgment language.

verses.text: “How Sheshach is taken! How the praise of the whole earth is seized! How Babylon has become a desolation among the nations!
verses.arminianNotes: “How Sheshach is taken! How the praise of the whole earth is seized!” Arminian readers see Sheshach used in parallel with Babylon, lamenting the fall of the world’s pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise take Sheshach as a name for Babylon, as the parallel line shows. Many interpreters explain it as a coded form of Babylon’s name, though readers in this tradition hold that explanation with caution.

verses.text: The sea has come up on Babylon. She is covered with the multitude of its waves.
verses.arminianNotes: “The sea has come up on Babylon. She is covered with the multitude of its waves.” Arminian readers see invading armies pictured as an overwhelming flood.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the flood image of judgment. Readers in this tradition note the poetic irony that a city built on waters is overwhelmed by a sea of enemies.

verses.text: Her cities have become a desolation, a dry land, and a desert, a land in which no man dwells. No son of man passes by it.
verses.arminianNotes: “Her cities have become a desolation, a dry land, and a desert.” Arminian readers see the flood image turned to drought, both expressing complete ruin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see total desolation. Readers in this tradition note that the mixing of flood and desert images shows that the poem is concerned with the certainty of judgment rather than literal sequence.

verses.text: I will execute judgment on Bel in Babylon, and I will bring out of his mouth that which he has swallowed up. The nations will not flow any more to him. Yes, the wall of Babylon will fall.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will execute judgment on Bel in Babylon, and I will bring out of his mouth that which he has swallowed up.” Arminian readers see Babylon’s god forced to give up what it took.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment on Bel, the god of Babylon. Readers in this tradition note the echo of 51:34, where Nebuchadnezzar swallowed Zion; now what was swallowed is restored.
